paper_sections.title: Similar neural mechanisms for perceptual guesses and free decisions

description.value: The study investigated whether perceptual guesses and free decisions share neural representations by using fMRI-based multivariate pattern classification to cross-predict decisions between the two conditions.

spans.text: Here we directly investigated whether perceptual guesses share brain networks with other types of free decisions.

design.value: Event-related fMRI study with three decision conditions: high-visibility perceptual categorization, zero-visibility perceptual guessing, and free choice between piano and chair categories.

spans.text: Here, we conducted an event-related fMRI study in which participants made category choices about pianos and chairs using three different conditions.

We trained an fMRI-based pattern classifier to distinguish between two perceptual guesses and tested whether it was able to predict the outcome of similar non-perceptual choices, as in conventional free choice tasks.
Here, we conducted an event-related fMRI study in which participants made category choices about pianos and chairs using three different conditions.
Participants indicated their choice by pressing one of two response buttons (right index- and middle finger), pseudo-randomized presented on either side of the fixation cross (2000 ms).
The parameter estimates for each voxel position formed the basis of subsequent searchlight decoding analyses for choices in all three conditions.
Trials were assigned to piano- and chair-trials according to participants' choices in all three conditions (HVC, PGC, FDC) in separate analyses.
Sixteen right-handed participants with normal or corrected to normal visual acuity gave written informed consent and participated in the study.

stimuli.value: 24 pictures of pianos and chairs; two scrambled masks; and a scrambled-phase noise image for the invisibility condition.

spans.text: The stimuli were 24 pictures of pianos and chairs, created from freely available pictures from the Internet or custom-made photographs, showing objects in different natural backgrounds ( ).
The average hit rate for both visible pianos (85.2%) and chairs (91.5%) was very high, indicating that the sensory information was used to make decisions ( ).

Additionally, response time data confirmed that free decision responses were given significantly faster ( p = .0016) than responses for perceptual guessing, providing evidence that participants could distinguish well between tasks ( B).

description.value: Participants were told that an object stimulus was presented, but only a strongly masked neutral noise image was shown, creating a zero-visibility perceptual guessing condition.

spans.text: For the perceptual guessing condition, only the noise image was shown, also preceded by a 150 ms pre-mask, then presented for 16.7 ms, and followed by a post-mask (500 ms minus target duration = 483.3 ms) ( ).
The use of noise stimuli guaranteed that participants' decisions were pure guesses or free choices (for pianos or chairs), without residual visibility influencing either process.
